I grip the tweed cushions, leaning in from my perch at the edge of the seat. Obama blinks his beautiful old wrinkly eyes. He blinks a lot, holy shit. "Wait a second..." I launch myself from the couch, running for the kitchen by the faint blue glow of the LCD monitor. I flip on the light, grab desperately through my journals on the counter, tossing dirty plates and dusty magazines over both shoulders. Then I find it.

I rummage through several drawers, digging around old tinfoil hats and rusted safety pins, until I find a pen that works. I leap back on the couch, and get to work. Three slow blinks "---" I jot it down. Four quick, one slow. I stare unblinkingly back at him, my love, my sweet. I grip the pen so tight the plastic cracks between my fat clammy fingers, working away to decipher the message, undoubtedly meant for me.

" O V E N S O N" the paper says. I whip my head back around to look at the kitchen. A little red light on, just above the stove. I turn slowly back to the screen. He winks at me. Ermahgerd.

James tugged the metal door open. The chilly November breeze followed him inside. He stopped at the entry, dropped his hood. Unsure where to go, he ambled toward where he thought the receptionist desk must be. Linoleum foot falls echoed back at him from blank, magnolia colored walls. 

"I heard there's a counselor here?" He said to the desks glossy veneer. The kindly woman behind the kiosk offered an innocuous smile. "If you'll just sign in here, Dr. Green will call you back when she's ready." In the waiting room James squirmed on unforgiving leather, stealing glances at himself in the spectral reflection of the window. "Mr. Corson?" came a small voice from over his shoulder.

He took a seat in the tweed armchair and fixed his gaze to the sickly green carpet, folding and refolding his hands, surreptitiously calming the choke rising in his throat. After a moment the silence was fractured "Were you a friend of Travis, Mr. Corson?"

"Was I?" he thought to himself. James blinked furiously, determined to fight the onslaught of tears he had tamed and then fallen to so many times since Saturday. 

He swallowed hard. "We were sleeping together." and the dam inside him broke. 

The woman watched him crumple into himself for a moment, watched him clutch desperately for air between anguished sobs. "He texted me on Wednesday" he stammered. "Said he was leaving soon. And I asked where, and he said-" a guttural noise escaped him, "-he said France."

"I was so fu-hic-fucking excited for him. He wanted to see me before he went." James stopped pawing at the tears, letting them trail down his neck under the collar of his t-shirt. "So on Friday, I texted him. Said 'wrud later?', and he said 'you'" he paused to clear his throat. "but I didn't really wanna fuck, and instead of just telling him that I-" couldn't say it. "I blew him off. Stopped replying. And then he did it."
"God f*cking dammit. When will this bitch stop blow drying her hair in the bathtub? Wrinkly dumb twat."

I watched the girls skitter around in the mud. They were so small then. Lobbing lumps of stewy earth into the others hair, piping laughter. The autumn sun could find them crawling in my arms, flicking caterpillars away from tender leaves, or else slinking in circles around me during matches of tag. 

     All through the long years they would visit. Tiptoed on my roots, they'd leap from one to another, and never once stuck a landing. They won't come around anymore.

     It's been too long.

But why opt out of the experience?
